items.title: William Russell Interview, 1976-02-16
items.q: they had to get people like Clarence Williams, at least in later days, to write down the tunes

ctx.x: That he improvises better or something like that. I don't...

You'd have a hard time making that argument stick, though, too, with a person like Louis, who learned to read very well, I guess, in the 20s on the boat, and then even took lessons in Chicago. And, of course, Bunk always could probably read quite well ever since he started. In fact, that's the way Bunk advised us starting in music. First in the solfège, as they call it, the old European classical sight reading and ear training, where you have to learn to sing the melodies just by looking at them without playing…
No. Was Buddy Bolden a reader? Did anyone know?

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-08-31
items.q: I'll get something about Clarence Williams, which was done in New York.

ctx.x: There's also a lot of material there that's invaluable. And we ought to be sure and get recorded some way.
Yes, that's why I'm making notes on the tape so that you'll know you'll get something from the people. I'll get something about Clarence Williams, which was done in New York.
Mrs. Rankin's supposed to keep after me.
